problems.problem: Prove that $46^{2n+1}+296\cdot 13^{2n+1}$ is divisible by $1947$.
Show that any graph with $6$ vertices contains a triangle or three vertices no two of which are joined.
What is the smallest number of discs of radius $\frac12$ that can cover a disc of radius $1$?
Knowing that 23 October 1948 was a Saturday, which is more frequent for New Year's Day, Sunday or Monday?
A convex polyhedron has no diagonals (every pair of vertices is connected by an edge). Prove that it is a tetrahedron.
Prove that among any $n$ positive integers one can always find some (at least one) whose sum is divisible by $n$.
Prove that $\sin x+\frac12\sin 2x+\frac13\sin 3x>0$ for $0^\circ<x<180^\circ$.

$P$ is a point on the base of an isosceles triangle. Lines through $P$ parallel to the sides meet the sides at $Q$ and $R$. Show that the reflection of $P$ in the line $QR$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle.
Which positive integers cannot be represented as a sum of (two or more) consecutive positive integers?

Several people visited a library yesterday. Each one visited the library just once (in the course of yesterday). Amongst any three of them, there were two who met in the library. Prove that there were two moments $T$ and $T'$ yesterday such that everyone who visited the library yesterday was in the library at $T$ or $T'$ (or both).

Three circles $C_1$, $C_2$, $C_3$ in the plane touch each other (in three different points). Connect the common point of $C_1$ and $C_2$ with the other two common points by straight lines. Show that these lines meet $C_3$ in diametrically opposite points.

$(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ are triples of real numbers such that for every pair of integers $(m,n)$ at least one of the numbers $x_1m+y_1n+z_1$, $x_2m+y_2n+z_2$ is an even integer. Prove that one of the triples consists of three integers.

$ABCD$ is a square. $E$ is a point on the side $BC$ such that $BE=\frac13 BC$, and $F$ is a point on the ray $DC$ such that $CF=\frac12 DC$. Prove that the lines $AE$ and $BF$ intersect on the circumcircle of the square.
For which $m>1$ is $(m-1)!$ divisible by $m$?

An open half-plane is the set of all points lying to one side of a line, excluding the points on the line itself. If four open half-planes cover the plane, show that one can select three of them which still cover the plane.

A circle $C$ touches three pairwise disjoint circles whose centres are collinear and none of which contains any of the others. Show that its radius must be larger than the radius of the middle one of the three circles.
Show that if we choose any $n+2$ distinct numbers from the set $\{1,2,3,\dots,3n\}$, there will be two whose difference is greater than $n$ and smaller than $2n$.

$ABC$ is a triangle. The point $A'$ lies on the side $BC$ and $BA'/BC=k$, where $\frac12<k<1$. Similarly, $B'$ lies on the side $CA$ with $CB'/CA=k$, and $C'$ lies on the side $AB$ with $AC'/AB=k$. Show that the perimeter of $A'B'C'$ is less than $k$ times the perimeter of $ABC$.
$A$ and $B$ are any two subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}$ such that $|A|+|B|>n-1$. Prove that one can find $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ such that $a+b=n$.
$n$ and $d$ are positive integers such that $d$ divides $2n^2$. Prove that $n^2+d$ cannot be a perfect square.
$ABCDEF$ is a convex hexagon with all its sides equal. Also $\angle A+\angle C+\angle E=\angle B+\angle D+\angle F$. Show that $\angle A=\angle D$, $\angle B=\angle E$ and $\angle C=\angle F$.
$ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral with $AB+BD=AC+CD$. Prove that $AB<AC$.
Every planar section of a three-dimensional body $B$ is a disc. Show that $B$ must be a ball.

A tournament is arranged amongst a finite number of people. Every person plays every other person just once and each game results in a win for one of the players (there are no draws). Show that there must be a person $X$ such that, given any other person $Y$ in the tournament, either $X$ beat $Y$, or $X$ beat $Z$ and $Z$ beat $Y$ for some $Z$.
Prove that if the two angles at the base of a trapezoid are different, then the diagonal starting from the vertex of the smaller angle is longer than the other diagonal.
How many five-digit numbers are divisible by $3$ and contain the digit $6$?

The vertices of a triangle are lattice points (they have integer coordinates). There are no other lattice points on the boundary of the triangle, but there is exactly one lattice point inside the triangle. Show that it must be the centroid.

$ABC$ is an acute-angled triangle. $D$ is a variable point in space such that all faces of the tetrahedron $ABCD$ are acute-angled. $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to the plane $ABC$. Find the locus of $P$ as $D$ varies.

A factory produces several types of mug, each with two colours, chosen from a set of six. Every colour occurs in at least three different types of mug. Show that we can find three mugs which together contain all six colours.
What is the largest possible value of $|a_1-1|+|a_2-2|+\dots+|a_n-n|$, where $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ is a permutation of $1,2,\dots,n$?
Given any six points in the plane, no three collinear, show that we can always find three which form an obtuse-angled triangle with one angle at least $120^\circ$.
Show that if $m$ and $n$ are integers such that $m^2+mn+n^2$ is divisible by $9$, then they must both be divisible by $3$.
The hexagon $ABCDEF$ is convex and its opposite sides are parallel. Show that the triangles $ACE$ and $BDF$ have equal area.

Among any four people at a party there is one who has met the three others before the party. Show that among any four people at the party there must be one who has met everyone at the party before the party.

Let $a_1=1,a_2,a_3,\dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that $$a_k<1+a_1+a_2+\dots+a_{k-1}$$ for all $k>1$. Prove that every positive integer can be expressed as a sum of distinct terms $a_i$.

$E$ is the midpoint of the side $AB$ of the square $ABCD$, and $F$, $G$ are points on the sides $BC$, $CD$ such that $EF$ is parallel to $AG$. Show that $FG$ touches the inscribed circle of the square.
Given any four distinct points in the plane, show that the ratio of the largest to the smallest distance between two of them is at least $\sqrt2$.
$x$, $y$, $z$ are positive reals less than $1$. Show that at least one of $(1-x)y$, $(1-y)z$ and $(1-z)x$ does not exceed $\frac14$.

Two circles with centres $O$ and $O'$ are disjoint. $PP'$ is a common outer tangent (with $P$ on the circle with centre $O$ and $P'$ on the circle with centre $O'$). Similarly, $QQ'$ is a common inner tangent (with $Q$ on the circle with centre $O$ and $Q'$ on the circle with centre $O'$). Show that the lines $PQ$ and $P'Q'$ meet on the line $OO'$.
Show that the number of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ of positive integers with least common multiple $n$ is the same as the number of positive divisors of $n^2$.
Show that given any $n+1$ diagonals of a convex $n$-gon, one can always find two which have no common point.
$P$ is any point of the tetrahedron $ABCD$ other than $D$. Show that at least one of the three distances $DA$, $DB$, $DC$ exceeds at least one of the distances $PA$, $PB$ and $PC$.

$mn$ students all have different heights. They are arranged in $m>1$ rows of $n>1$. In each row select the shortest student and let $A$ be the height of the tallest of these. In each column select the tallest student and let $B$ be the height of the shortest of these. Which of the following are possible: $A<B$, $A=B$, $A>B$? If a relation is possible, can it always be realized by a suitable arrangement of the students?
$A$ is an acute angle. Show that $$\left(1+\frac{1}{\sin A}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{\cos A}\right)>5.$$
A triangle has no angle greater than $90^\circ$. Show that the sum of its medians is greater than four times its circumradius.

$ABC$ is an equilateral triangle. $D$ and $D'$ are points on opposite sides of the plane $ABC$ such that the two tetrahedra $ABCD$ and $ABCD'$ are congruent (but not necessarily with the vertices in that order). If the polyhedron with the five vertices $A,B,C,D,D'$ is such that the angle between any two adjacent faces is the same, find $DD'/AB$.

At a party every girl danced with at least one boy, but not with all of them. Similarly, every boy danced with at least one girl, but not with all of them. Show that there were two girls $G$ and $G'$ and two boys $B$ and $B'$ such that $B$ and $G$ danced, $B'$ and $G'$ danced, but $B$ and $G'$ did not dance, and $B'$ and $G$ did not dance.
Show that for any positive reals $w,x,y,z$ we have $$\sqrt{\frac{w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2}{4}}\ge\sqrt[3]{\frac{wxy+wxz+wyz+xyz}{4}}.$$
Which integers $a,b,c$ satisfy $a^2+b^2+c^2+3<ab+3b+2c$?
$D$ is a closed disc of radius $R$. Show that among any $8$ points of $D$ one can always find two whose distance apart is less than $R$.

A pyramid has a square base and equal lateral edges. It is cut into two parts by a plane parallel to the base. The lower part (which has a square top and a square base) is such that the circumcircle of its base is smaller than the circumcircles of its lateral faces. Show that the shortest path on the surface joining the two endpoints of a space diagonal of this lower part lies entirely on the lateral faces.
Can we arrange $5$ points in space to form a pentagon with equal sides such that the angle between each pair of adjacent edges is $90^\circ$?
Show that the first $n$ digits after the decimal point of $(5+\sqrt{26})^n$ are all equal.
Do there exist two infinite sets $A$ and $B$ of non-negative integers such that every non-negative integer can be uniquely represented in the form $a+b$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$?
$A$ is a set of integers which is closed under addition and contains both positive and negative numbers. Show that the difference of any two elements of $A$ also belongs to $A$.

A convex $n$-gon is divided into triangles by diagonals which do not intersect except at vertices of the $n$-gon. Each vertex belongs to an odd number of triangles. Show that $n$ must be a multiple of $3$.

For a vertex $X$ of a quadrilateral, let $h(X)$ be the sum of the distances from $X$ to the two sides not containing $X$. Show that if a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ satisfies $h(A)=h(B)=h(C)=h(D)$, then it must be a parallelogram.
In an infinite sequence of positive integers every term (starting with the second) is the harmonic mean of its neighbours. Show that all the numbers must be equal.

There are $4n$ segments of unit length inside a circle of radius $n$. Show that given any line $L$ there is a chord of the circle parallel or perpendicular to $L$ which intersects at least two of the $4n$ segments.

For each arrangement $X$ of $n$ white and $n$ black balls in a row, let $f(X)$ be the number of times the colour changes as one moves from one end of the row to the other. For each $k$ such that $0<k<n$, show that the number of arrangements $X$ with $f(X)=n-k$ is the same as the number with $f(X)=n+k$.
Show that if $2+2\sqrt{28n^2+1}$ is an integer (for $n$ an integer), then it is a perfect square.
A triangle has side lengths $a,b,c$ and opposite angles $A,B,C$. Show that if $$a(1-2\cos A)+b(1-2\cos B)+c(1-2\cos C)=0,$$ then the triangle is equilateral.

We are given $64$ cubes, each with five white faces and one black face. One cube is placed on each square of a chessboard, with its edges parallel to the sides of the board. We are allowed to rotate a complete row of cubes about the axis of symmetry running through the cubes, or to rotate a complete column of cubes about the axis of symmetry running through the cubes. Show that by a sequence of such rotations we can always arrange that each cube has its black face uppermost.
What is the largest possible number of acute angles in an $n$-gon which is not self-intersecting (no two non-adjacent edges intersect)?
A valid lottery ticket is formed by choosing $5$ distinct numbers from $1,2,3,\dots,90$. What is the probability that the winning ticket contains at least two consecutive numbers?

$n$ points are taken in the plane, no three collinear. Some of the line segments between the points are painted red and some are painted blue, so that between any two points there is a unique path along coloured edges. Show that the uncoloured edges can be painted (each edge either red or blue) so that all triangles have an odd number of red sides.

A straight line cuts the side $AB$ of the triangle $ABC$ at $C_1$, the side $AC$ at $B_1$ and the line $BC$ at $A_1$. $C_2$ is the reflection of $C_1$ in the midpoint of $AB$, and $B_2$ is the reflection of $B_1$ in the midpoint of $AC$. The lines $B_2C_2$ and $BC$ intersect at $A_2$. Prove that $$\frac{\sin\angle B_1A_1C}{\sin\angle C_2A_2B}=\frac{B_2C_2}{B_1C_1}.$$

Given any $22$ points in the plane, no three collinear, show that the points can be divided into $11$ pairs so that the $11$ line segments defined by the pairs have at least five different intersection points.

There are $30$ boxes, each with a unique key. The keys are randomly arranged in the boxes, so that each box contains just one key, and the boxes are locked. Two boxes are broken open, thus releasing two keys. What is the probability that the remaining boxes can be opened without forcing them?
A triangle has side lengths $a,b,c$. Prove that $$a(b-c)^2+b(c-a)^2+c(a-b)^2+4abc>a^3+b^3+c^3.$$

A class has $n>1$ boys and $n$ girls. For each arrangement $X$ of the class in a line, let $f(X)$ be the number of ways of dividing the line into two non-empty segments so that in each segment the number of boys and girls is equal. Let the number of arrangements with $f(X)=0$ be $A$, and the number of arrangements with $f(X)=1$ be $B$. Show that $B=2A$.

$ABCD$ is a square of side $10$. There are four points $P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4$ inside the square. Show that we can always construct line segments parallel to the sides of the square, of total length $25$ or less, so that each $P_i$ is linked by the segments to both of the sides $AB$ and $CD$. Show that for some points $P_i$ it is not possible with a total length less than $25$.
For which positive integers $n,k$ (with $k<n$) are the binomial coefficients $$\binom{n}{k-1},\quad\binom{n}{k},\quad\binom{n}{k+1}$$ three successive terms of an arithmetic progression?
For any positive real $r$, let $d(r)$ be the distance from the circle with centre at the origin and radius $r$ to the nearest lattice point. Show that $d(r)$ tends to zero as $r$ tends to infinity.

$n>4$ planes are in general position (every $3$ planes have exactly one common point, and no point belongs to more than $3$ planes). Show that there are at least $\frac{2n-3}{4}$ tetrahedra among the regions formed by the planes.

A library has one exit and one entrance, and a blackboard at each. Only one person enters or leaves at a time. As he does so, he records on the blackboard the number of people he finds in (when entering) or leaves in (when leaving) the library. Prove that at the end of the day exactly the same numbers will be found on the two blackboards (possibly in a different order).
$S_n$ is a square of side $\frac1n$. Find the smallest $k$ such that the squares $S_1,S_2,S_3,\dots$ can be put into a square of side $k$ without overlapping.
Let $$p_k(x)=1-x+\frac{x^2}{2!}-\frac{x^3}{3!}+\dots+\frac{(-x)^{2k}}{(2k)!}.$$ Show that $p_k(x)$ is non-negative for all real $x$ and all positive integers $k$.
Transform the equation $$ab^2\left(\frac{1}{(a+c)^2}+\frac{1}{(a-c)^2}\right)=a-b$$ into a simpler form, given that $a>c\ge 0$ and $b>0$.
Prove or disprove: given any quadrilateral inscribed in a convex polygon, we can find a rhombus inscribed in the polygon with side not less than the shortest side of the quadrilateral.
$ABCD$ is a parallelogram. $P$ is a point outside the parallelogram such that the angles $\angle PAB$ and $\angle PCB$ have the same value but opposite orientation. Show that $\angle APB=\angle DPC$.

A lottery ticket is a choice of $5$ distinct numbers from $1,2,3,\dots,90$. Suppose that $5^5$ distinct lottery tickets are such that any two of them have a common number. Prove that one can find four numbers such that every ticket contains at least one of the four.
Prove that if the quadratic $x^2+ax+b$ is always positive (for all real $x$), then it can be written as the quotient of two polynomials whose coefficients are all positive.
Show that there are no integers $n$ such that $n^4+4^n$ is a prime greater than $5$.

$ABC$ is a triangle with orthocentre $H$. The median from $A$ meets the circumcircle again at $A_1$, and $A_2$ is the reflection of $A_1$ in the midpoint of $BC$. The points $B_2$ and $C_2$ are defined similarly. Show that $H$, $A_2$, $B_2$ and $C_2$ lie on a circle.
Three schools each have $n$ students. Each student knows a total of $n+1$ students at the other two schools. Show that there must be three students, one from each school, who know each other.
$a$ and $b$ are rationals. Show that if $ax^2+by^2=1$ has a rational solution (in $x$ and $y$), then it must have infinitely many.

The vertices of a convex $n$-gon are coloured so that adjacent vertices have different colours. Prove that if $n$ is odd, then the polygon can be divided into triangles by non-intersecting diagonals such that no diagonal has endpoints of the same colour.
A triangle has inradius $r$ and circumradius $R$. Its longest altitude has length $H$. Show that if the triangle does not have an obtuse angle, then $H\ge r+R$. When does equality hold?

The base of a convex pyramid has an odd number of edges. The lateral edges of the pyramid are all equal, and the angles between neighbouring lateral faces are all equal. Show that the base must be a regular polygon.
$f$ is a real-valued function defined on the reals such that $f(x)\le x$ and $f(x+y)\le f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x,y$. Prove that $f(x)=x$ for all $x$.
An $n\times n$ array of letters is such that no two rows are the same. Show that it must be possible to omit a column so that the remaining table has no two rows the same.
The points of space are coloured with five colours, with all colours being used. Prove that some plane contains four points of different colours.

Let $n>1$ be an odd integer. Prove that a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of positive integers $x$ and $y$ satisfying $$\frac{4}{n}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}$$ is that $n$ has a prime divisor of the form $4k-1$.

In a certain country there are two tennis clubs consisting of $1000$ and $1001$ members respectively. All the members have different playing strengths, and the descending order of playing strengths in each club is known. Find a procedure which determines, within $11$ games, who is in the $1001$st place among the $2001$ players in these clubs. It is assumed that a stronger player always beats a weaker one.
Prove that $$AB+PQ+QR+RP\le AP+AQ+AR+BP+BQ+BR,$$ where $A,B,P,Q$ and $R$ are any five points in a plane.

Let $n>2$ be an even number. The squares of an $n\times n$ chessboard are coloured with $\frac12 n^2$ colours in such a way that every colour is used for exactly two of the squares. Prove that one can place $n$ rooks on squares of $n$ different colours such that no two of the rooks can take each other.
For a positive integer $n$, let $r(n)$ denote the sum of the remainders when $n$ is divided by $1,2,\dots,n$ respectively. Prove that $r(k)=r(k-1)$ for infinitely many positive integers $k$.
A cube with integer edge length is placed in space so that all four vertices of one of its faces are lattice points. Prove that the other four vertices are also lattice points.

Prove that for any integer $k>2$ there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that the least common multiple of $n,n+1,\dots,n+k-1$ is greater than the least common multiple of $n+1,n+2,\dots,n+k$.

The set of integers is coloured in $100$ colours in such a way that all the colours are used and the following holds: for any intervals $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ of equal length with integer endpoints, if $a$ and $c$ as well as $b$ and $d$, respectively, have the same colour, then the intervals $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ are identically coloured, that is, for any integer $x$ with $0\le x\le b-a$ the numbers $a+x$ and $c+x$ have the same colour. Prove that $-1982$ and $1982$ are of different colours.
Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be rational numbers satisfying $$x^3+3y^3+9z^3-9xyz=0.$$ Prove that $x=y=z=0$.
The polynomial $f(x)=x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\dots+a_{n-1}x+1$ has non-negative coefficients and $n$ real roots. Prove that $f(2)\ge 3^n$.

Given are $n+1$ points $P_1,P_2,\dots,P_n$ and $Q$ in the plane, no three collinear. For any two different points $P_i$ and $P_j$ there is a point $P_k$ such that the point $Q$ lies inside the triangle $P_iP_jP_k$. Prove that $n$ is an odd number.

Write down the first $4$ rows of Pascal's triangle in the usual (centred) way and add up the numbers in each vertical column; we obtain $7$ numbers. If we repeat this procedure with the first $1024$ rows of Pascal's triangle, how many of the $2047$ numbers thus obtained will be odd?

$A_1B_1A_2$, $B_1A_2B_2$, $A_2B_2A_3$, $\dots$, $B_{13}A_{14}B_{14}$, $A_{14}B_{14}A_1$ and $B_{14}A_1B_1$ are equilateral rigid plates that can be folded along the edges $A_1B_1$, $B_1A_2$, $\dots$, $A_{14}B_{14}$ and $B_{14}A_1$ respectively. Can they be folded so that all $28$ plates lie in the same plane?

Given are $n$ integers, not necessarily distinct, and two positive integers $p$ and $q$. If the $n$ numbers are not all distinct, choose two equal ones; add $p$ to one of them and subtract $q$ from the other. If there are still equal ones among the $n$ numbers, repeat this procedure. Prove that after a finite number of steps all $n$ numbers are distinct.

We have triangulated a convex $(n+1)$-gon $P_0P_1\dots P_n$ (i.e., divided it into $n-1$ triangles by $n-2$ non-intersecting diagonals). Prove that the resulting triangles can be labelled with the numbers $1,2,\dots,n-1$ such that for every $i\in\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}$, $P_i$ is a vertex of the triangle with label $i$.

For every positive integer $n$, define the power sum of $n$ as follows. For every prime divisor $p$ of $n$, consider the largest positive integer $k$ for which $p^k\le n$, and add up all these $p^k$. (For instance, the power sum of $100$ is $2^6+5^2=89$.) Prove that the power sum of $n$ is larger than $n$ for infinitely many positive integers $n$.
We reflect each vertex of a triangle in the opposite side. Prove that the area of the triangle formed by these three reflected points is smaller than five times the area of the original triangle.

Any two members of a club with $3n+1$ people play ping-pong, tennis or chess with each other. Everyone has exactly $n$ partners with whom he plays ping-pong, $n$ with whom he plays tennis and $n$ with whom he plays chess. Prove that we can choose three members of the club who play three different games amongst each other.

Let $n>2$ be a positive integer. Find the largest value $h$ and the smallest value $H$ for which $$h<\frac{a_1}{a_1+a_2}+\frac{a_2}{a_2+a_3}+\dots+\frac{a_n}{a_n+a_1}<H$$ holds for any positive reals $a_1,\dots,a_n$.

$A$ and $B$ play the following game: they choose randomly $k$ integers from $\{1,2,\dots,100\}$; if their sum is even, $A$ wins, otherwise $B$ wins. For which values of $k$ do $A$ and $B$ have the same chance of winning?

Prove that if there exists a point $P$ inside the convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ such that the triangles $PAB$, $PBC$, $PCD$, $PDA$ have the same area, then one of the diagonals of $ABCD$ bisects the area of the quadrilateral.

A set $T\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}^3$ has the property that every triple $(a,b,c)\in T$ satisfies $a<b<c$, and for any two triples $(a,b,c)$ and $(x,y,z)$ in $T$ at most one of the equalities $a=x$, $b=y$, $c=z$ holds. Find the maximum of $|T|$.

Consider a convex lattice quadrilateral $PQRS$ whose diagonals intersect at $E$. Prove that if $\angle P+\angle Q<180^\circ$, then the triangle $PQE$ contains, inside it or on one of its sides, a lattice point other than $P$ and $Q$.

In the plane, two intersecting lines $a$ and $b$ are given, along with a circle $\omega$ that has no common points with these lines. For any line $\ell\parallel b$, define $A=\ell\cap a$, and $\{B,C\}=\ell\cap\omega$ such that $B$ is on segment $AC$. Construct the line $\ell$ for which the ratio $\frac{|BC|}{|AB|}$ is maximal.
For any positive integer $n$ denote by $S(n)$ the digit sum of $n$ in the decimal system. Find every positive integer $M$ for which $S(Mk)=S(M)$ holds for all integers $1\le k\le M$.

We play the following game in a Cartesian coordinate system in the plane. From the point $(x,y)$, in one step we may move to the point $(x,y\pm 2x)$ or to the point $(x\pm 2y,y)$. There is an additional rule: it is not allowed to make two consecutive steps that lead back to the same point (i.e., to step backwards). Prove that starting from the point $\left(1,\sqrt2\right)$, we cannot return to it in finitely many steps.
Let $p>2$ be a prime number and $n$ a positive integer. Prove that $pn^2$ has at most one positive divisor $d$ for which $n^2+d$ is a perfect square.

The incentre of $\triangle A_1A_2A_3$ is $I$, and the centre of the $A_i$-excircle is $J_i$ ($i=1,2,3$). Let $B_i$ be the intersection point of the side $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ and the bisector of $\angle A_{i+1}IA_{i+2}$ (indices modulo $3$). Prove that the three lines $B_iJ_i$ are concurrent.

We would like to give a present to one of $100$ children. We do this by throwing a biased coin $k$ times, after deciding in advance who wins for each possible outcome. Prove that we can choose the probability $p$ of throwing heads and the value of $k$ such that, by distributing the $2^k$ different outcomes between the children in the right way, each child has the same probability of winning.
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $a,b\ge 1$, $c>0$ be arbitrary real numbers. Prove that $$\frac{(ab+c)^n-c}{(b+c)^n-c}\le a^n.$$

A convex polyhedron has two triangular and three quadrilateral faces. Connect every vertex of one of the triangular faces with the intersection point of the diagonals of the quadrilateral face opposite to it. Show that the resulting three lines are concurrent.

Consider $998$ red points in the plane, no three collinear. We select $k$ blue points in such a way that inside each triangle whose vertices are red points there is a blue point as well. Find the smallest $k$ for which such a selection of blue points is possible for any configuration of $998$ red points.

For $n$ given positive reals, define their strange mean as the sum of their squares divided by their sum. Decide which of the following statements holds for $n=2$:

a) The strange mean is never smaller than the third power mean.

b) The strange mean is never larger than the third power mean.

c) The strange mean, depending on the given numbers, can be larger or smaller than the third power mean.

Which statement is valid for $n=3$?
For any positive integer $k$ define $f_1(k)$ as the square of the digit sum of $k$ in the decimal system, and $f_n(k)=f_1(f_{n-1}(k))$ for all $n>1$. Compute $f_{1992}(2^{1991})$.

Consider finitely many points in the plane, no three collinear. Prove that we can colour the points with two colours such that there is no half-plane that contains exactly three of the points with those three points all of the same colour.
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers. Prove that the numbers $an^2+b$ and $a(n+1)^2+b$ are both perfect squares only for finitely many integers $n$.

Triangle $ABC$ is not isosceles. The incircle of $\triangle ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at the points $K$, $L$, $M$. The parallel to $LM$ through $B$ meets $KL$ at $D$, and the parallel to $LM$ through $C$ meets $KM$ at $E$. Prove that $DE$ passes through the midpoint of $LM$.
Let $n$ be a fixed positive integer. Find the minimum over $\mathbb{R}$ of the polynomial $$f(x)=\sum_{t=0}^{2n}(2n+1-t)x^t.$$
The ratio of the sides of a parallelogram is $\lambda>1$. Given $\lambda$, determine the maximum of the acute angle between the diagonals of the parallelogram.

Prove that if we erase $n-3$ diagonals of a regular $n$-gon, then we may still choose $n-3$ of the remaining diagonals such that no two of them intersect inside the $n$-gon; but it is possible to erase $n-2$ diagonals such that this statement does not hold.

Consider the sets $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n$, where $A_k$ is the union of $k$ disjoint intervals of the real axis ($k=1,2,\dots,n$). Prove that from the intervals forming these sets one can choose $\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\right\rfloor$ intervals that belong to pairwise different sets $A_k$ and no two of which have a common point.

In the plane, a lattice rectangle with sides parallel to the coordinate axes is divided into lattice triangles of area $\frac12$. Prove that the number of right-angled triangles among them is at least twice the length of the shorter side of the rectangle. (A lattice polygon is a polygon both coordinates of each of whose vertices are integers.)

Consider a polynomial in $n$ variables with real coefficients. We know that if every variable is $\pm1$, the value of the polynomial is positive if the number of $-1$'s is even, and negative if it is odd. Prove that the degree of this polynomial is at least $n$.

Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are such that no three of them are collinear. Let $E=AB\cap CD$ and $F=BC\cap DA$. Let $k_1$, $k_2$ and $k_3$ denote the circles with diameters $AC$, $BD$ and $EF$, respectively. Prove that either $k_1,k_2,k_3$ pass through one point, or no two of them intersect.
Prove that in a trapezoid with perpendicular diagonals, the product of the legs is at least the product of the bases.

Let $n$ and $k$ be arbitrary non-negative integers. Suppose we have drawn $2kn+1$ (different) diagonals of a convex $n$-gon. Show that there exists a broken line formed by $2k+1$ of these diagonals that passes through no point more than once. Prove also that this is not necessarily true when we draw only $kn$ diagonals.
Let $p>2$ be a prime number and let $L=\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}^2$. Prove that we can find $p$ points in $L$ with no three of them collinear.

The centre of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ is $O$, its incentre is $I$, and its intouch triangle is $A_1B_1C_1$. Let $H_1$ be the orthocentre of $\triangle A_1B_1C_1$. Prove that $O$, $I$ and $H_1$ are collinear.
Prove that the vertices of any planar graph can be coloured with $3$ colours such that there is no monochromatic cycle.

Is there an infinite sequence of positive integers in which no two terms are relatively prime, no term divides any other term, and there is no integer larger than $1$ that divides every term of the sequence?
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a polynomial with integer coefficients whose values at the points $1,2,\dots,n$ are pairwise different powers of $2$.

For which integers $N\ge 3$ can we find $N$ points in the plane, no three collinear, such that for any triangle formed by three vertices of the convex hull of the points there is exactly one of the points inside that triangle?

For any positive integer $m$, denote by $d_i(m)$ the number of positive divisors of $m$ that are congruent to $i$ modulo $2$. Prove that if $n$ is a positive integer, then $$\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(d_0(k)-d_1(k)\right)\right|\le n.$$
Given a triangle in the plane, construct inside the triangle the point $P$ for which the centroid of the triangle formed by the three projections of $P$ onto the sides of the triangle is $P$ itself.

We are given more than $2^k$ integers, where $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Prove that we can choose $k+2$ of them such that if some of the selected numbers satisfy $$x_1+x_2+\dots+x_m=y_1+y_2+\dots+y_m,$$ where $x_1<\dots<x_m$ and $y_1<\dots<y_m$, then $x_i=y_i$ for every $1\le i\le m$.
Colour the lattice points of $L=\{0,1,\dots,n\}^2$ red or green in such a way that every unit lattice square in $L$ has exactly two red vertices. How many such colourings are possible?

Let $ABC$ be a non-equilateral triangle in the plane, and let $T$ be a point different from its vertices. Define $A_T$, $B_T$ and $C_T$ as the second intersection points of the lines $AT$, $BT$ and $CT$ with the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that there are exactly two points $P$ and $Q$ in the plane for which the triangles $A_PB_PC_P$ and $A_QB_QC_Q$ are equilateral. Prove furthermore that the line $PQ$ passes through the circumcentre of $\triangle ABC$.

Let $k\ge 0$ be an integer and suppose that the integers $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ give at least $2k$ different residues upon division by $n+k$. Show that there are some $a_i$ whose sum is divisible by $n+k$.
$3n-1$ points are given in the plane, no three collinear. Prove that one can select $2n$ of them whose convex hull is not a triangle.

Let $k\ge 3$ be an integer. Prove that if $n>\binom{k}{3}$, then for any $3n$ pairwise different real numbers $a_i,b_i,c_i$ ($1\le i\le n$), among the numbers $a_i+b_i$, $a_i+c_i$, $b_i+c_i$ one can find at least $k+1$ pairwise different numbers. Show that this is not always the case when $n=\binom{k}{3}$.
In a square lattice take a lattice triangle that has the smallest area among all the lattice triangles similar to it. Prove that the circumcentre of this triangle is not a lattice point.

We have an acute-angled triangle which is not isosceles. We denote its orthocentre, circumcentre and incentre by $H$, $O$, $I$ respectively. Prove that if a vertex of the triangle lies on the circle $HOI$, then another vertex lies on this circle as well.

The Fibonacci sequence is defined by $f_1=f_2=1$, $f_{n+2}=f_{n+1}+f_n$ ($n\in\mathbb{N}$). Suppose that $a$ and $b$ are positive integers such that $\frac ab$ lies between the two fractions $\frac{f_n}{f_{n-1}}$ and $\frac{f_{n+1}}{f_n}$. Show that $b\ge f_{n+1}$.
Prove that the edges of a complete graph with $3^n$ vertices can be partitioned into disjoint cycles of length $3$.

Draw a circle $k$ with diameter $EF$, and let $e$ be its tangent at $E$. Consider all possible pairs $A,B\in e$ for which $E$ lies on the segment $AB$ and $AE\cdot EB$ is a fixed constant. Let $A_1$ and $B_1$ be the second intersection points of $AF$ and $BF$ with $k$. Prove that all the segments $A_1B_1$ pass through one point.

Prove that if a graph $\mathcal{G}$ on $n\ge 3$ vertices has a unique $3$-colouring, then $\mathcal{G}$ has at least $2n-3$ edges.

(A graph is $3$-colourable when there exists a colouring of its vertices with $3$ colours such that no two vertices of the same colour are joined by an edge. The graph can be $3$-coloured uniquely if there do not exist vertices $u$ and $v$ that are coloured differently in one $3$-colouring, yet coloured the same in another.)
Prove that the following inequality holds for all but finitely many positive integers $n$: $$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\gcd(i,j)>4n^2.$$

Given are a triangle $ABC$, its circumcircle $\omega$, and a circle $k$ that touches $\omega$ from the outside and also touches the rays $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that the $A$-excentre of $\triangle ABC$ is the midpoint of $PQ$.

Find the smallest positive integer $n\neq 2004$ for which there exists a polynomial $f$ with integer coefficients such that the equation $f(x)=2004$ has at least one integer solution and the equation $f(x)=n$ has at least $2004$ different integer solutions.

We have placed some red and blue points along a circle. The following operations are permitted:

(a) we may add a red point somewhere and switch the colours of its neighbours;

(b) we may remove a red point from somewhere and switch the colours of its neighbours (if there are at least $3$ points on the circle).

Initially there are two blue points on the circle. Using a number of these operations, can we reach a state with exactly two red points?

Let $N>1$ and let $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_N$ be nonnegative reals with sum at most $500$. Prove that there exist integers $k\ge 1$ and $1=n_0<n_1<\dots<n_k=N$ such that $$\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_ia_{n_{i-1}}<2005.$$

$A$ and $B$ play tennis. The first player to win at least four points and at least two more than the other player wins the game. We know that $A$ wins each point with probability $p\le\frac12$, independently of the game so far. Prove that the probability that $A$ wins the game is at most $2p^2$.

We build a tower of $2\times 1$ dominoes in the following way. First, we place $55$ dominoes on the table so that they cover a $10\times 11$ rectangle; this is the first storey of the tower. We then build every new level with $55$ dominoes covering the same $10\times 11$ rectangle. The tower is called stable if for every non-lattice point of the $10\times 11$ rectangle we can find a domino that has an inner point above it. What is the smallest number of storeys of a stable tower?

Is there a set $S\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ of $2006$ points such that not all its points are coplanar, no three of the points are collinear, and for any $A,B\in S$ we can find points $C,D\in S$ for which $AB\parallel CD$?

Let $a,t,n$ be positive integers such that $a\le n$. Consider the subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ any two elements of which differ by at least $t$. Prove that the number of such subsets not containing $a$ is at most $t^2$ times the number of those that do contain $a$.

We deal $n-1$ cards in some way to $n$ people sitting around a table. From then on, in one move a person with at least $2$ cards gives one card to each of his or her neighbours. Prove that eventually a state will be reached where everyone has at most one card.

We have placed $n>3$ cards around a circle, face down. In one step we may perform the following operation with three consecutive cards: calling the middle one $B$ and the two at the ends $A$ and $C$, we put card $C$ in the place of $A$, and move $A$ and $B$ to the places originally occupied by $B$ and $C$, respectively; meanwhile, we flip the cards $A$ and $B$. Using a number of these steps, is it possible to move each card to its original place, but face up?

Prove that if from any $2007$ consecutive terms of an infinite arithmetic progression of integers starting with $2$ one can choose a term relatively prime to all the $2006$ other terms, then also among any $2008$ consecutive terms there is a term relatively prime to the rest.
Denote by $d(n)$ the number of positive divisors of a positive integer $n$. Find the smallest constant $c$ for which $d(n)\le c\sqrt n$ holds for all positive integers $n$.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $a_1<a_2<\dots<a_n$ be integers. Let $S$ be the set of pairs $1\le i<j\le n$ for which $a_j-a_i$ is a power of $2$, and $T$ the set of pairs $1\le i<j\le n$ for which $j-i$ is a power of $2$. (Here the powers of $2$ are $1,2,4,\dots$.) Prove that $|S|\le|T|$.

In a far-away country, travel between cities is only possible by bus or by train. One can travel by train or by bus only between certain cities, and the rides do not necessarily go in both directions. We know that for any two cities $A$ and $B$, one can reach $B$ from $A$, or $A$ from $B$, using only bus rides or only train rides. Prove that there exists a city from which every other city can be reached using only one type of vehicle (but different cities may be reached with different vehicles).

Let $n,k$ be arbitrary positive integers. We fill the entries of an $n\times k$ array with integers such that each of the $n$ rows contains the integers $1,2,\dots,k$ in some order. Add up the numbers in each of the $k$ columns, and let $S$ be the largest of these sums. What is the minimal possible value of $S$?

Find all pairs $(a,b)$ of positive integers for which the set of positive integers can be partitioned into sets $H_1$ and $H_2$ such that neither $a$ nor $b$ can be represented as the difference of two numbers in $H_i$, for $i=1,2$.

Find all functions $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ with the following properties: if $f(x)<c<f(y)$ for some rational $c$, then $f$ takes the value $c$; and $$f(x)+f(y)+f(z)=f(x)f(y)f(z)$$ whenever $x+y+z=0$.

We have $n$ keys, each of them belonging to exactly one of $n$ locked chests. Our goal is to decide which key opens which chest. In one try we may choose a key and a chest, and check whether the chest can be opened with the key. Find the minimal number $p(n)$ with the property that using $p(n)$ tries we can surely discover which key belongs to which chest.

Consider a triangle $ABC$ with points $A_1$, $A_2$ on side $BC$, $B_1,B_2$ on side $AC$ and $C_1,C_2$ on side $AB$ such that $AC_1<AC_2$, $BA_1<BA_2$, $CB_1<CB_2$. Let the circles $AB_1C_1$ and $AB_2C_2$ meet at $A$ and $A^*$. Similarly, let the circles $BC_1A_1$ and $BC_2A_2$ meet at $B^*\neq B$, and let the circles $CA_1B_1$ and $CA_2B_2$ meet at $C^*\neq C$. Prove that the lines $AA^*$, $BB^*$, $CC^*$ are concurrent.

For which positive integers $n$ and $k$ do there exist integers $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ and $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_k$ such that the products $a_ib_j$ ($1\le i\le n$, $1\le j\le k$) give pairwise different residues modulo $nk$?

Let $a_1,a_2,\dots$ be an infinite sequence of positive integers such that for any positive integers $k,\ell$, $a_{k+\ell}$ is divisible by $\gcd(a_k,a_\ell)$. Prove that for any integers $1\le k\le n$, the product $a_na_{n-1}\cdots a_{n-k+1}$ is divisible by $a_ka_{k-1}\cdots a_1$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Denote by $a(n)$ the number of ways of writing $n=x_1+x_2+\dots$, where $x_1\le x_2\le\dots$ are positive integers and $x_i+1$ is a power of $2$ for each $i$. Denote by $b(n)$ the number of ways of writing $n=y_1+y_2+\dots$, where the $y_i$ are positive integers and $2y_i\le y_{i+1}$ for each $i$. Prove that $a(n)=b(n)$.

Given $2n$ points and $3n$ lines in the plane, prove that there is a point $P$ in the plane such that the sum of the distances from $P$ to the $3n$ lines is less than the sum of the distances from $P$ to the $2n$ points.

Let $J_A$ and $J_B$ be the $A$-excentre and $B$-excentre of $\triangle ABC$. Consider a chord $PQ$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$ which is parallel to $AB$ and intersects the segments $AC$ and $BC$. If the lines $AB$ and $CP$ intersect at $R$, prove that $$\angle J_AQJ_B+\angle J_ARJ_B=180^\circ.$$

Denote by $E(n)$ the number of $1$'s in the binary representation of a positive integer $n$. Call $n$ interesting if $E(n)$ divides $n$. Prove that

(a) there cannot be five consecutive interesting numbers, and

(b) there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $n$, $n+1$ and $n+2$ are all interesting.

Consider $n$ events, each of which has probability $\frac12$. We also know that the probability of any two of them both happening is $\frac14$. Prove the following.

(a) The probability that none of these events happens is at most $\frac{1}{n+1}$.

(b) Equality in (a) can be attained for infinitely many $n$.

Let $a,b$ be positive real numbers satisfying $2ab=a-b$. For any positive integer $k$, let $x_k$ and $y_k$ be the integers closest to $ak$ and $bk$, respectively (if there are two closest integers, choose the larger one). Prove that a positive integer $n$ appears in the sequence $(x_k)_{k\ge1}$ if and only if it appears at least three times in the sequence $(y_k)_{k\ge1}$.

Consider closed polygonal discs $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ with the property that for any three points $A\in P_1$, $B\in P_2$, $C\in P_3$ we have $[\triangle ABC]\le 1$, where $[X]$ denotes the area of the polygon $X$.

(a) Prove that $\min\{[P_1],[P_2],[P_3]\}<4$.

(b) Give an example of polygons $P_1,P_2,P_3$ with the above property such that $[P_1]>4$ and $[P_2]>4$.

Is it true that for every integer $n\ge 2$ and any non-negative reals $\ell_{ij}$, $1\le i<j\le n$, we can find non-negative numbers $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ such that $|a_i-a_j|\ge\ell_{ij}$ for all $1\le i<j\le n$, and yet $$\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\le\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\ell_{ij}?$$

A society has $n$ members, each of whom knows at least one but at most $n - 2$ of the others; acquaintance is always mutual. Prove that four suitably chosen members of the society can be seated around a table so that each of them knows exactly one of his two neighbours at the table.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle, and let $P$ be a point in the interior of the triangle which does not lie on any of the altitude lines of the triangle. Denote the feet of the altitudes from the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ by $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$, respectively. Let the rays $AP$, $BP$, $CP$ meet the circumcircle of the triangle at the points $A_2$, $B_2$, $C_2$, respectively. Prove that the circles $AA_1A_2$, $BB_1B_2$ and $CC_1C_2$ pass through one point.

Let $K$ be a closed convex polygonal region and $X$ a point in the plane of $K$. Show that $X$ can be brought into the interior or onto the boundary of the polygonal region $K$ by a succession of finitely many reflections in certain side lines of $K$, performed in a suitable order, if reflections in the same side line may be performed several times.

In fencing, you win a bout if you are the first to reach $15$ points. Suppose that when $A$ fences against $B$, at any point during the bout, $A$ scores the next point with probability $p$ and $B$ scores the next point with probability $q=1-p$ (they never both score at the same time). Suppose that in this bout $A$ already has $14-k$ points and $B$ has $14-\ell$ points (where $0\le k,\ell\le 14$). By how much does the probability that $A$ wins the bout increase if $A$ scores the next point?

Consider a triangle $ABC$ and a point $D$ on its side $AB$. Let $I$ be a point inside $\triangle ABC$ on the angle bisector of $\angle ACB$. The second intersections of the lines $AI$ and $CI$ with the circle $ACD$ are $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Similarly, the second intersections of the lines $BI$ and $CI$ with the circle $BCD$ are $R$ and $S$, respectively. Show that if $P\neq Q$ and $R\neq S$, then the lines $AB$, $PQ$ and $RS$ pass through one point or are parallel.

Let $Q=\{0,1\}^n$, and let $A$ be a subset of $Q$ with $2^{n-1}$ elements. Prove that there are at least $2^{n-1}$ pairs $(a,b)\in A\times(Q\setminus A)$ for which the sequences $a$ and $b$ differ in exactly one term.

Let $1\le k\le n$ be integers. At most how many $k$-element subsets can we select from $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ such that for any two selected subsets, one of them consists of the $k$ smallest elements of their union?
If $p,q\in\mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfy $p(p(x))=q(x)^2$, does it follow that $p(x)=r(x)^2$ for some $r\in\mathbb{R}[x]$?

Let $ABC$ be an arbitrary triangle, and choose the points $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$ independently of each other, with uniform distribution, on the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$, respectively. For a point $Z$ of the plane, let $p(Z)$ denote the probability that the triangle bounded by the lines $AA'$, $BB'$ and $CC'$ contains $Z$. Determine the interior point $Z$ of the triangle $ABC$ for which $p(Z)$ is as large as possible.
Are there polynomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ with real coefficients for which the polynomial $f(x)^3 - g(x)^2$ has degree one?

A number is written into each cell of an $n \times n$ table $T$ so that no number occurs twice in any row. Prove that the numbers in $T$ can be rearranged so that after the rearrangement every row of the table $T^*$ contains exactly the same numbers as the corresponding row of $T$, but no number occurs twice in any column of $T^*$.

The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$, respectively, and the median from $A$ meets the segment $B_1C_1$ at the point $M$. Prove that the segment $A_1M$ is perpendicular to the side $BC$.

Let $\underline{v}_1, \underline{v}_2, \dots, \underline{v}_n$ be pairwise distinct vectors of length $p$ with integer coordinates in the three-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system, where $p$ is a prime. Suppose that for any $1 \le j < k \le n$ there is an integer $0 < \ell < p$ such that all three coordinates of the vector $\underline{v}_j - \ell \cdot \underline{v}_k$ are divisible by $p$. Prove that $n \le 6$.

In the village of Aprajafalva, which consists of $k$ streets, there are $k(n-1)+1$ clubs, each with exactly $n$ dwarf members. A dwarf may be a member of several clubs, and two dwarfs certainly know each other if they are members of a common club or if they live in the same street. Prove that one can select $n$ different clubs and one member from each of them such that these $n$ members are pairwise different and any two of them know each other.

In the acute triangle $ABC$, $AB < AC < BC$, and the feet of the altitudes from the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ are $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$, respectively. Let $P$ be the reflection of the point $C_1$ in the line $BB_1$, and let $Q$ be the reflection of the point $B_1$ in the line $CC_1$. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $A_1PQ$ passes through the midpoint of the side $BC$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Determine all families $\mathcal{F}$ consisting of certain subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ such that for every fixed nonempty $X \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, the number of sets $A \in \mathcal{F}$ for which $|A \cap X|$ is even equals the number of sets $A \in \mathcal{F}$ for which $|A \cap X|$ is odd.

Is it true that if $H$ and $A$ are bounded subsets of the real line, then $H$ can be decomposed into pairwise disjoint translated copies of $A$ in at most one way? (Infinitely many translated copies are also allowed.)

Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers. We are given $n$ closed discs in the plane such that whichever $k+1$ of them we choose, there are always two chosen discs that have no common point. Prove that the $n$ discs can be partitioned into at most $10k$ classes such that no two discs in the same class have a common point.

Determine all functions $f$ defined on the set of rational numbers with nonnegative real values such that for all rational numbers $x$, $y$:

$f(x+y) \le f(x) + f(y)$,

$f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$,

$f(2) = 1/2$.

There are $N$ houses in a town. Every Christmas, Santa Claus visits all the houses in some order. Prove that if $N$ is large enough, then in any three consecutive years one can always find $13$ houses which (among the three years) were visited in the same order in two of the years. Determine the smallest $N$ for which this holds.

The origin $O = (0,0)$ is an interior point of the triangle formed by the points $P_i = (a_i, b_i)$ $(i = 0, 1, 2)$ of the Cartesian plane. Prove that the areas of the triangles $P_0OP_1$, $P_0OP_2$, $P_1OP_2$ (in this order) form a geometric progression if and only if the system of equations
$$a_0x^2 + a_1x + a_2 = b_0x^2 + b_1x + b_2 = 0$$
has a real solution $x$.

In Wonderland, $n$ airlines operate flights between $n$ cities. Each airline is associated with an odd number of cities, say $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_i$, between which it operates a round-trip service in both directions: tickets can be bought for the flights $v_jv_{j+1}$ and $v_{j+1}v_j$ for $1 \le j \le i$, where $v_{i+1} = v_1$. Prove that one can find an odd number of cities, say $u_1, u_2, \dots, u_k$, such that tickets for the flights $u_1u_2, u_2u_3, \dots, u_{k-1}u_k, u_ku_1$ can be bought from pairwise different airlines.

We are given a cyclic hexagon $A_1B_3A_2B_1A_3B_2$ whose diagonals $A_1B_1$, $A_2B_2$ and $A_3B_3$ pass through one point. For each $i = 1, 2, 3$, let $C_i$ be the intersection point of the diagonals $A_iB_i$ and $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$, and let $D_i$ be the point, different from $B_i$, on the circumcircle of the hexagon such that the circle $B_iC_iD_i$ is tangent to the line $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$. (Points are indexed modulo $3$, i.e. $A_4 = A_1$ and $A_5 = A_2$.) Prove that the segments $A_1D_1$, $A_2D_2$ and $A_3D_3$ pass through one point.

A square has been divided into $2022$ rectangles (such that no two of the rectangles have a common interior point). Consider all lines containing the sides of all the rectangles. At most how many different lines can we get?

Suppose that for the primes $p$, $q$ which leave remainder $3$ when divided by $4$, the equation $x^2 - pqy^2 = 1$ has a solution in positive integers $x$, $y$. Prove that the equation $|px^2 - qy^2| = 1$ also has a solution in positive integers $x$, $y$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that if the real numbers $a_{i,j}$ $(1 \le i, j \le n)$ satisfy $a_{i,j} + a_{j,i} = 0$ for all $i$, $j$ (in particular, $a_{i,i} = 0$ for all $i$), then the following inequality holds:
$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{i,j}\right)^2 \le \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{i,j}^2.$$
When does equality hold?

Let $f(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_ix^i$, where $d \ge 1$, the coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_d$ are nonnegative integers and $a_d > 0$. Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $f(n)$ is not divisible by any of the numbers $f(2), f(3), \dots, f(n-1)$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Call the points of the Cartesian plane both of whose coordinates are among the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ vertices. Call the segments of unit length both of whose endpoints are vertices edges. Some edges have been coloured red so that between any two distinct vertices there is exactly one red path (polygonal line). A red edge $f$ is called important for the edge $e$ if the red path connecting the two endpoints of $e$ passes through $f$. Prove that there is a red edge which is important for at least $n$ edges.

We are given a convex cyclic pentagon $ABCDE$ and an interior point $P$ such that $AB = AE = AP$ and $BC = CE$. The lines $AD$ and $BE$ meet at $Q$. The points $R$ and $S$ lie on the segments $CP$ and $BP$, respectively, such that $DR = QR$ and $SR \parallel BC$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $BEP$ and $PQS$ are tangent to each other.

The quadrilateral $ABCD$ has been divided into cyclic quadrilaterals no two of which have a common interior point. None of the vertices of the cyclic quadrilaterals of the division lies in the interior of a side of another cyclic quadrilateral of the division or in the interior of a side of the quadrilateral $ABCD$. Prove that $ABCD$ is also a cyclic quadrilateral.

The ancient One-Dimensional Empire lay along a line. Initially there were no cities. A total of $n$ different point-like cities were founded one by one; from the second one on, each newly founded city and the already existing city closest to it (if there were two such cities, then the older one) were declared twin cities.

The surviving map of the empire shows the cities and the distances between them, but not the order in which they were founded. Historians try to conclude from the map that each city had at most $41$ twin cities.

(a) For $n = 106$, give a map from which this conclusion can be drawn.

(b) Prove that for $n = 1013$ this conclusion cannot be drawn from any map.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $H \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}$ be a nonempty set. Suppose that for every element $a \in H$ there are elements $b \in H$ and $c \in H$, different from $a$, such that $b + c - 2a$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that $p < 4k$, where $k$ denotes the number of elements of the set $H$.

Let $n$ be a fixed positive integer. The numbers $0,1,\dots,n-1$ are written on a board in some order. Two numbers form an inversion if the larger one precedes the smaller one. A number $k$ is called peculiar if it forms an inversion with exactly $k$ other numbers. At most how many peculiar numbers can there be on the board?

In this problem numbers are written in base $10$, and representations beginning with zeros are allowed. A number with an even number of digits is called cuttable if, when it is cut into two parts of equal length, the square of the sum of the two parts equals the original number. For example, $2025=(20+25)^2$ and $0001=(00+01)^2$ are four-digit cuttable numbers. Prove that for every $n$ the number of $2n$-digit cuttable positive integers is a power of $2$.

Given $n\ge 10$ points in the plane, no three of them on a line. Prove that the points can be coloured red and blue so that every half-plane containing at least $10$ of the points contains both a red and a blue point.
